          Xabi Alonso Has ‘No Explanation’, So Why Are Chelsea Scoring So Many Early Goals?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 14, 2026
          
                      Ali Tweedale / Author, Emily Millen / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Chelsea have started the Xabi Alonso era by scoring a remarkable number of goals very early on in their games. Why do they start so well, and why do they then fade?
Even though they’ve done it so many times already, it is still a surprise every time Chelsea repeat the trick.

On Saturday, Xabi Alonso’s side went into their meeting with Bournemouth having scored three goals in the opening five minutes of their first five league games this season. The other 19 Premier League teams had just two such goals between them.
And yet, it was still a shock to see them add to their total, but largely because of how they did it.

For starters, they didn’t just score once within the first five minutes of the game, but twice. And they didn’t just do it inside five minutes, but inside three. With goals from Jordan Henderson and Morgan Rogers by the time the clock read 2:29, Chelsea had raced into the third-earliest 2-0 lead in Premier League history (after Leicester vs Derby in April 1998 and Luton vs Brighton in January 2024).

Given Alonso’s reign had begun with João Pedro’s goal after 31 seconds of the season opener against Fulham, Roméo Lavia’s fourth-minute goal against Brighton, and Rogers’ second-minute strike at Arsenal, subsequent opponents might have been well advised to set up with Chelsea’s fast starts in mind. But they scored inside seven minutes against Hull and then twice within the first three minutes against Bournemouth.

The problem for their opponents is there is no pattern to follow. Chelsea don’t attack in a particular way from the early stages. There isn’t some single thing or theme that future opponents should be looking out for.

In fact, only once this season have Chelsea started off with a clear intention to put their opponents on the back foot by booting the ball straight out from kick-off for a throw-in deep in opposition territory. That was the 3-0 defeat at Brentford, the only game in which Chelsea didn’t score an early goal (or score at all for that matter).

Their manager insists there is no gameplan to start quickly, no intention to begin games with a focus on scoring early. “I have nothing to do with it, so I don’t have the answer,” Alonso said after the win over Bournemouth. “I have no explanation, so I can take no credit.”

Rogers disagrees. “I put it down to the manager’s team talks,” the midfielder said after he scored against Bournemouth this weekend, his third goal inside the first seven minutes of a Premier League game since joining Chelsea.
“He gets us firing, gets us going,” he continued. “We always want to start off on the front foot. It is about starting well and getting the lead.
“A lot of games, especially at home, we have won after jumping on the back of early goals. It’s a good trait to have which we need to keep doing.”
Alonso may not realise he is doing it, but Rogers’ comments suggest the manager is having an impact with his pre-game words.

Also, there may well be a feeling of momentum among the players. Reports from inside the dressing room suggest there is confidence they can score an early goal, and joking among the players as to who is going to score it, not as to whether the team will get one at all.
Whatever the reason, what's certain is the impressive volume of early goals and the efficiency with which they are finishing off chances at the start of games.

They have four goals inside the first three minutes of Premier League games this season, while the other 19 teams have just two between them. Chelsea’s four goals in this time have come from just five shots and 0.71 xG. The two goals scored by everyone else have been scored almost perfectly in line with the expected goals value of the shots (1.92 xG).
Inside the first five minutes of games, they have five goals from 1.52 xG. Expand things to the opening 15 minutes, and they have seven goals from 2.28 xG.

Chelsea have outperformed their xG so comprehensively early on because their early goals have almost exclusively been difficult chances. João Pedro’s goal at Fulham was a gorgeous chipped finish over the goalkeeper. Rogers’ strike at Arsenal was a volley from the edge of the area, while his opener against Hull was a fine low finish from the corner of the box. And both early goals against Bournemouth last weekend were from distance with several opponents in the way.

Perhaps Chelsea players feel at the start of games that they have more licence to shoot from distance, emboldened to take things on that they might not later in games because there is less pressure to make their chances count. And this, along with the confidence that Alonso gives them could just be an effective combination.

Clearly, Chelsea also have an abundance of talented attacking players, all of whom have started the season in form, and it might just be a coincidence that they are performing so well early on in games.
